message.content:
Since \(m \equiv 6 \pmod 9\), we know \(m\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(9\).

Also, \(n \equiv 0 \pmod 9\), so \(n\) is divisible by \(9\).

Thus every product \(mn\) is at least divisible by
\[
3\cdot 9 = 27.
\]

Now check whether any larger integer is always guaranteed. Consider the smallest valid choices:
\[
m=6,\quad n=9 \implies mn=54.
\]
Also,
\[
m=15,\quad n=9 \implies mn=135.
\]
The greatest common divisor of \(54\) and \(135\) is
\[
\gcd(54,135)=27.
\]
So no divisor larger than \(27\) can divide every possible \(mn\).

Therefore, the largest integer that \(mn\) is necessarily divisible by is
\[
\boxed{27}.
\]

The answer is 27.
